A **negotiation** is any conversation where two or more people who need something from each other try to reach an agreement. You negotiate when you buy fabric in Balogun market, when a customer asks for a discount on a cake order, when you agree a delivery date with a supplier, when you discuss rent with a landlord and when you talk about pay with an employer. You also negotiate at home, about school fees, chores or who travels for a family event. It is not a talent some people are born with. It is a set of habits you can learn and practise.

Positions versus interests

The most useful idea in this course comes from the book **Getting to Yes** by Roger Fisher, William Ury and Bruce Patton of the Harvard Negotiation Project. They noticed that people usually argue over **positions**: the specific thing each side says it wants. 'I want ₦50,000.' 'I will only pay ₦40,000.' A position is the answer a person has already chosen.

Behind every position sits an **interest**: the need, worry or goal that made the person choose that position. Interests answer the question **why**. A supplier who demands full payment upfront may be worried about customers who never pay. A customer who wants a lower price may have a fixed budget from her church committee. A landlord who wants two years' rent may need money for a building project. When you only argue about positions, one person must lose. When you understand interests, you can often find an option that satisfies both.

The four principles
Getting to Yes sets out four principles. Learn them in plain words:
**Separate the people from the problem.** You can be soft on the person and firm on the issue. Respect the trader, the boss or the landlord as a human being while you discuss the money.
**Focus on interests, not positions.** Ask why, listen, and share your own interests too.
**Invent options for mutual gain.** Before deciding, list several possible deals: different payment timing, bigger quantity, added service, longer contract.
**Insist on objective criteria.** Use fair standards both sides can check, such as current market prices, a written price list, what similar shops charge, or the cost of materials.
Worked example: a bulk order of ankara bags

For example, Ngozi sews ankara tote bags in Enugu. A school administrator, Mrs Bello, wants 60 bags for a graduation and offers ₦3,000 each. Ngozi's normal price is ₦4,500 and each bag costs her about ₦2,800 in fabric, lining, thread and transport (approximate prices).
Positions: Mrs Bello says ₦3,000. Ngozi wants ₦4,500. The gap is ₦1,500 a bag, or ₦90,000 on 60 bags.

Ngozi asks: 'Can you tell me a bit about the budget and what the bags are for?' Mrs Bello explains the parents' association approved ₦200,000 in total and the bags must be ready in three weeks with the school logo.
Ngozi now knows the interest: stay inside ₦200,000 and get branded bags on time. ₦200,000 divided by 60 is about ₦3,333 a bag.

Ngozi proposes options: (a) 60 bags without inner pocket at ₦3,300 each = ₦198,000; (b) 50 full bags at ₦4,000 each = ₦200,000; (c) 60 full bags at ₦4,000 if the school pays the extra ₦40,000 next term.
Mrs Bello chooses option (a). Ngozi's profit is about ₦500 a bag, ₦30,000 in total, and she gets a repeat customer.
By asking why, Ngozi turned a ₦1,500 argument into a choice between three workable deals. The school stayed within budget and Ngozi kept a profit she was happy with.
Two magic questions

When someone gives you a firm demand, ask 'Help me understand what is important to you about that?' and later 'What if we did it this way?' The first uncovers the interest, the second tests an option without forcing anyone to commit.
Why this works

Most people come into a negotiation expecting a fight. When you show real interest in their situation, they relax and share information they would normally hide. That information, the deadline, the budget limit, the fear of late payment, is what lets you design a better deal. You are not being soft. You are collecting the facts you need to make a strong, smart offer.

In the rest of this module you will add two more tools: knowing exactly when to walk away, and knowing your own habits under pressure. Together with interests, these form the base of every negotiation you will practise in this course.

The term **BATNA** was introduced in Getting to Yes. Your BATNA is not a wish. It is a real option you could take tomorrow. If a buyer will not pay your price for 20 crates of tomatoes, your BATNA might be selling them to another buyer at Mile 12 market for a known price. Your walk-away point comes from your BATNA: never accept a deal worse than your best alternative.
The ZOPA: where a deal is possible

The **ZOPA** (Zone Of Possible Agreement) is the range between the seller's walk-away point and the buyer's walk-away point. If the seller will go down to ₦80,000 and the buyer will go up to ₦95,000, any price from ₦80,000 to ₦95,000 is possible. If the seller's minimum is higher than the buyer's maximum, there is no ZOPA on price and you must change something else (quantity, quality, timing) or walk away politely.

A deal can only happen between the two walk-away points; skill decides where inside that range it lands.
Worked example: selling a used chest freezer

For example, Halima in Kaduna is selling a used chest freezer. A neighbour offered ₦120,000 last week and will still buy it this month. A small restaurant owner, Chinedu, has asked about it (approximate prices).
Halima's BATNA: sell to the neighbour for ₦120,000. So her walk-away point is ₦120,000.
She checks similar freezers on Jiji and with two repairers: similar sizes in good condition are advertised around ₦150,000 to ₦170,000. She sets her target at ₦155,000.

Chinedu privately decides he will pay up to ₦145,000, because a new one costs far more and a repairer offered him a different used one for ₦145,000. That is his BATNA, so ₦145,000 is his walk-away point.
ZOPA = ₦120,000 to ₦145,000. Halima's target of ₦155,000 is outside it, but she does not know that yet.
Halima opens at ₦160,000 and shows the freezer working. Chinedu offers ₦125,000. After discussion they settle at ₦140,000, with Chinedu arranging his own transport.
The deal at ₦140,000 sits inside the ZOPA. Halima earned ₦20,000 more than her BATNA because she knew her numbers and did not panic when the first offer came in low.
Make your BATNA stronger before you negotiate
The person with the better alternative usually has more power. You can improve yours before you sit down:
Get at least two other quotes or buyers. Ask three suppliers for prices on WhatsApp before you visit the one you prefer.
Know the real market price from several sources: other traders, online listings, a friend in the trade.
Prepare a fallback plan: another apartment, another job application, another customer group.
Think about the other side's BATNA too. If they have few alternatives, you have more room.
Do not move your walk-away point in the heat of the moment

Pressure, a friendly smile or 'last price, take it now' can make you drop your limit. Only change your walk-away point if you learn genuinely new facts, and if you need to, ask for a short break to think.
When there is no ZOPA

Sometimes, after honest discussion, the numbers simply do not overlap. That is useful information, not a defeat. You have three choices. First, change the package: a smaller quantity, a simpler finish, a later delivery date or a longer contract can bring the numbers together. Second, test whether the other side's limit is real: 'What would need to change for you to reach ₦130,000?' Third, walk away politely and take your BATNA. What you should not do is accept a deal below your walk-away point just because you have already spent time talking. Time spent is gone either way; a bad deal keeps costing you.
Keep your walk-away point private. Saying 'my lowest is ₦120,000' usually means the deal ends at ₦120,000. Instead, give reasons and ranges that point toward your target.

The five conflict modes

A widely used model, the **Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument**, describes five styles based on two questions: how much you care about your own goals (assertiveness) and how much you care about the other person's goals (cooperativeness). No style is always right; the skill is choosing.

Worked example: choosing a style on purpose

For example, Funke runs a small provisions shop in Ibadan. She notices she always accommodates: last month she gave three regular customers credit worth ₦45,000 in total because she felt shy to refuse, and ₦30,000 of it is still unpaid.
She lists her negotiations for the week: a supplier price rise, a customer asking for credit, a neighbour asking to store goods in her shop.
Supplier price rise (₦300 more per carton of noodles, 10 cartons a week = ₦3,000 a week): she decides to collaborate, asking whether paying cash on delivery could keep the old price.
Customer asking for ₦8,000 credit: she chooses to be more assertive and offers a compromise of ₦3,000 credit, repaid by Friday, written in her credit book.
Neighbour storage request: small and friendly, she accommodates for one week only.
Funke reduced new credit risk from ₦8,000 to ₦3,000 and opened a real conversation with her supplier. She did not become harsh; she simply matched her style to each situation.
Safety and power
Some negotiations carry risk beyond money. Protect yourself first:
**Meet in public or familiar places** for first meetings with strangers, especially when buying or selling items found online. Take someone with you if you can.
**Never pay a deposit to someone you have not verified.** Fake landlords and agents ask for inspection or booking fees for properties they do not own. Confirm ownership and visit in person.
**Check payment alerts in your bank app**, not a screenshot or SMS the buyer shows you. Fake transfer alerts are a common trick.
**Protect your data.** Do not share your BVN, card PIN or one-time codes in any negotiation. No genuine buyer, landlord or employer needs your PIN.
**Watch for power imbalance.** If someone threatens you, uses family pressure to force a deal, or makes you feel unsafe, you can stop, leave and bring a trusted person or adviser.
You are allowed to pause
Saying 'Let me think about it and get back to you tomorrow' is always acceptable. Anyone who refuses to let you think overnight on a big decision is giving you a reason to be careful.
Emotions, confidence and gender expectations

Many women are raised to be agreeable and to avoid looking 'too forward' about money. This can make asking for a fair price, a raise or better terms feel uncomfortable. Remember that negotiating for a fair deal is a normal part of business and work, not rudeness. Two habits help. First, speak about the facts and your reasons, not your feelings: 'My price covers fabric, lining and two fittings' is calm and hard to argue with. Second, practise your key sentences beforehand, so that the words come out steadily even when you feel nervous.

Notice your body too. A fast heartbeat or a dry mouth before a negotiation is normal. Breathe slowly, sit or stand straight, and speak a little slower than usual. People tend to treat a calm, steady speaker as confident, even when she is nervous inside.

Finally, set one honest goal. If you usually accommodate, your goal might be 'state my price once without apologising'. If you usually compete, your goal might be 'ask two questions about their needs before making my offer'. Small, specific goals change habits faster than big promises.

Most negotiations are won or lost before anyone speaks. Twenty minutes of preparation with a pen and paper, or a note on your phone, will usually earn you more than an hour of clever talking. The seven-part preparation sheet
**Goal.** What do I want from this deal in one sentence? Include price, but also timing, quality and relationship.
**My interests.** Why do I want it? List your real needs, such as cash flow, reliability, school-run hours.
**Their interests.** What might they need? Guess, then plan questions to check.
**Numbers.** BATNA, walk-away point, target and the opening offer you will make.
**Objective standards.** Market prices, quotes, receipts, price lists, photos of quality, anything both sides can check.
**Tradeables.** Things you can give or ask for besides price: quantity, payment timing, delivery, packaging, referrals, contract length.
**Opening line and questions.** The first two sentences you will say and three questions you will ask.

Research in fifteen minutes

You do not need expensive data. Send the same short WhatsApp message to three suppliers or sellers: 'Good morning, please what is your price for 10 yards of guinea brocade, and do you deliver to Wuse?' Check online marketplaces such as Jiji for similar used items. Ask one trusted person in the trade what they paid recently. Write the lowest, highest and typical price you find. Prices in Nigeria move quickly, so evidence from this week is better than memory from last year.
Tradeables are your secret stock

A tradeable that is cheap for you but valuable to them is the best thing to offer. For a hair stylist, adding a free hair wash costs little but feels generous; for a supplier, a customer who pays on time every week is worth more than a small price increase.
Worked example: a preparation sheet for a flour supplier

For example, Aisha bakes bread and meat pies in Kano and buys 8 bags of flour a week. Her distributor has told her the price is going up from ₦68,000 to ₦74,000 a bag (approximate prices for illustration).
Goal: keep flour cost as low as possible while keeping reliable weekly delivery.
Her interests: cash flow, steady supply, no late deliveries. Supplier's likely interests: regular buyers, fast payment, lower delivery costs.

Numbers: the rise costs her 8 x ₦6,000 = ₦48,000 more a week. Two other distributors quote ₦72,000 and ₦73,500 but charge ₦5,000 delivery. Her BATNA is ₦72,000 + ₦5,000 delivery spread across 8 bags, about ₦72,625 a bag. Walk-away: ₦72,600. Target: ₦71,000. Opening: ₦70,000.
Tradeables: order 16 bags every two weeks instead of 8 weekly (fewer delivery trips), pay on delivery by transfer, collect from the depot herself.
Opening line: 'Thank you for always delivering on time. I want to keep buying from you. Can we look at how I order so the new price works for both of us?'

Aisha walks in knowing that anything above about ₦72,600 means she should switch, and she has three tradeables to offer. She settles at ₦71,500 for fortnightly orders of 16 bags, saving ₦2,500 a bag compared with the new list price, which is ₦40,000 over two weeks.
Plan your opening

Decide your first offer before the meeting, based on your target and your evidence, not on what feels comfortable in the moment. The next lesson explains why the first number has so much power. For now, write it down and write one reason that supports it, for example 'my price includes delivery and a one-week replacement guarantee'.
Prepare for their side too

Spend a few minutes sitting in the other person's chair. What pressures do they face this month? A supplier may have a loan to repay, a landlord may have a child's school fees due, an employer may be worried about losing a good worker. You will not know for sure, but writing down two or three guesses tells you which questions to ask and which tradeables may matter most to them. Also note what they might say to push back, and write your calm reply beside each objection.
Finally, rehearse. Say your opening line aloud twice, or practise with a friend playing the other side. Hearing yourself say a confident number makes it much easier to say it again when it matters.

Trade concessions instead of giving them away

In 1974 psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described **anchoring**: when people estimate a value, they are pulled toward the first number they see, even when that number is not very relevant. In negotiation the first serious offer often works as an anchor. The rest of the conversation tends to happen around it.
A bag of money
The first number on the table pulls the final price toward it.
Should you make the first offer?
**Go first when you have good information** about market prices. A well-supported first offer anchors the conversation in your favour.
**Let them go first when you know very little**, for example when buying an unusual item. Their number may be better than you expected, and you avoid anchoring against yourself.
**If they anchor first with an extreme number**, do not argue about it in detail. Say calmly, 'That is far from what the market shows,' and move straight to your own well-supported offer.
Set an ambitious but defensible opening

Open above your target when selling (below it when buying), but stay close enough that you can explain it with a reason. An opening that is wildly unrealistic can insult the other person and end the talk. In many Nigerian markets both buyer and seller expect some movement, so leave room to come down without going below your target. A useful habit is to state the number with its reason in the same breath: 'It is ₦25,000 because the fabric is pure cotton and I finish all seams by hand.'
Concession patterns
How you move matters as much as where you start. Big or equal steps tell the other side there is plenty more room. **Shrinking steps** tell them you are approaching your limit.
A shrinking concession pattern (selling)
Open at ₦50,000
Move to ₦46,000
Move to ₦44,000
Move to ₦43,000
Agree at ₦43,000
Each step is smaller than the last: ₦4,000, then ₦2,000, then ₦1,000, signalling the limit is near.
Worked example: selling a catering package

For example, Grace runs a small catering business in Port Harcourt. A client wants jollof rice, chicken and drinks for 100 guests. Grace's cost is about ₦380,000. Her walk-away is ₦430,000 and her target is ₦470,000 (approximate prices).
Grace opens at ₦520,000, explaining it includes servers, cooler hire and clean-up.
Client offers ₦400,000. Grace does not jump. She asks, 'What is your budget made up of?' The client says the family has agreed ₦460,000 maximum but also wants small chops.
Grace trades rather than gives: 'If you provide your own drinks, I can do ₦490,000.' (Drinks cost her about ₦35,000, so her margin is protected.)
Client asks for ₦460,000. Grace moves a smaller step: '₦475,000 with small chops for 100, if you pay 60% deposit this week.'
Client agrees at ₦470,000 with the 60% deposit (₦282,000) by Friday and the balance on the event morning.
Grace reached her target of ₦470,000. Every concession was traded for something (drinks removed, early deposit), and her steps shrank from ₦30,000 to ₦15,000 to ₦5,000, which signalled the end.
The 'if, then' rule

Never give a concession for nothing. Use the shape 'If you can [pay upfront / take 20 pieces / collect yourself], then I can [adjust the price].' This keeps the deal balanced and teaches the other side that every request has a cost.
Common mistakes
Revealing your walk-away point early ('my lowest is ₦430,000').
Splitting the difference automatically when the midpoint is below your target.
Making two concessions in a row without getting anything back.
Accepting the very first offer so fast that the other person feels they paid too much and starts asking for extras.
Responding to their anchor

When the other side opens with a number far from yours, the anchor still pulls at your thinking. Protect yourself by looking at your preparation sheet again before you reply, so your own target and evidence are fresh in your mind. Do not make a counter-offer that only moves a little from their extreme number, because that accepts their anchor as the starting point. Instead, name your own justified number and the reason behind it. If the gap is very large, ask them to explain how they arrived at their figure; often the explanation shows a mistake or an item you can remove.

Round numbers also send signals. A precise figure such as ₦47,500 sounds calculated and carefully considered, while ₦50,000 can sound like a guess with room to move. Use precise numbers when you have done the arithmetic and want your offer to be taken seriously.

The person who asks good questions usually learns more and decides better. Listening is not waiting quietly for your turn. It is collecting the information that will shape your offer, and showing the other person that you take their situation seriously.

Closed questions get yes or no. Open questions begin with what, how, or tell me, and invite real information. Useful examples:

'How did you arrive at that price?'
'What would need to be true for you to say yes?'
'What happens on your side if this is not ready by the 15th?'
'How are you planning to use it?'

Handling pushback
Worked example: a customer says 'Your price is too high'
For example, Ifeoma sells hand-made beaded necklaces at ₦12,000 each at a craft fair in Abuja. A buyer wants three for a wedding party and says the price is too high.
Ifeoma stays calm and mirrors: 'Too high?'
Buyer: 'Yes, I saw some for ₦7,000 online.' Ifeoma labels: 'It sounds like you want to be sure you are paying a fair price.'
She uses objective criteria: 'The ₦7,000 ones are usually plastic beads. These are glass beads with a metal clasp. Here, feel the weight.'
She asks an open question: 'What is your budget for the three?' Buyer: '₦30,000.'
Ifeoma offers a trade: 'If you take three, I will do ₦32,000 for all three and add matching earrings for the bride.' Earrings cost her about ₦1,200 in materials.
Buyer agrees and pays ₦32,000 by transfer; Ifeoma checks the alert in her own bank app before handing over the goods.

Instead of defending or dropping her price, Ifeoma listened, explained value and traded. She sold three necklaces for ₦32,000, a discount of ₦4,000 from ₦36,000, while gaining a satisfied bride's family as future customers.
Silence is a tool
After you state your price or ask a question, stop talking. Count slowly to five in your head. Many people fill the silence with useful information or a better offer.
Feedback and correction after each negotiation
Questions to avoid

Some questions make people defensive. 'Why are you so expensive?' sounds like an accusation. 'How did you arrive at that price?' asks for the same information in a respectful way. Leading questions such as 'You do want to keep me as a customer, don't you?' feel like pressure. Also avoid asking several questions at once; the other person will answer only the easiest one. Ask one clear question, then listen to the whole answer before you speak again.

Take short notes during important negotiations, such as a rent or salary talk. Write down numbers, dates and any promises. Tell the other person, 'Let me write that down so I do not forget,' which also shows that you take their words seriously. These notes become the basis of your written confirmation at the end, and they protect you if memories differ later.

Listening also works on the phone and on WhatsApp. In voice notes and messages, summarise what you understood before replying with your offer. A short line such as 'So you need 50 pieces by the 20th and would prefer to pay half now' prevents many costly mistakes.

Spend five minutes after every important negotiation answering four questions in your notebook: Did I end above my walk-away point? How close did I get to my target? Is the relationship still healthy? What will I do differently next time? Over several weeks, patterns appear. If you always finish near your walk-away point, practise holding your opening longer and making smaller concessions. If relationships often feel strained, spend more time asking and summarising before you state your position.

Suppliers and customers are the two sides of your business. Every naira you save when buying and every naira you protect when selling goes straight to your profit. These are also long-term relationships, so the aim is a deal that is good for you and that the other side is happy to repeat.

A low unit price can hide costs. Always compare suppliers on the **landed cost**: the price per unit plus delivery, packaging, losses from damaged goods and the cost of paying early. Then negotiate every part of the package, not just the price.

Worked example: comparing two fabric suppliers
For example, Rukayat makes school uniforms in Abeokuta and needs 200 yards of grey fabric (approximate prices).
Supplier A: ₦1,900 a yard, full payment upfront, ₦8,000 delivery. Landed cost = (200 x ₦1,900) + ₦8,000 = ₦388,000.
Supplier B: ₦1,950 a yard, free delivery, 50% upfront and 50% after delivery. Landed cost = 200 x ₦1,950 = ₦390,000.
B is only ₦2,000 more, and paying half later helps her cash flow while she waits for school payments.
Rukayat asks B: 'If I order 300 yards for the next two terms, can you do ₦1,880 a yard on the same payment terms?' B offers ₦1,900.
New landed cost for 300 yards with B: 300 x ₦1,900 = ₦570,000, with ₦285,000 paid now and ₦285,000 after delivery.
By comparing landed cost and negotiating payment timing and quantity, Rukayat gets A's unit price with B's better terms and stock for two terms.
With customers: protect your margin

Customers in Nigerian markets often ask 'What is the last price?' This is normal and friendly. Plan for it: build a little room into your opening price, know your cost and walk-away point for every product, and prefer giving value over cutting price.

**Know your break-even.** If a dress costs you ₦9,000 to make and you sell at ₦15,000, a ₦3,000 discount cuts your profit in half, from ₦6,000 to ₦3,000.
**Offer value, not cuts:** free delivery within your area, an extra small item, faster finishing, or a discount only for larger quantities.
**Use quantity breaks:** for example ₦15,000 each, or ₦42,000 for three.
**Agree deposits for custom work.** Many tailors, caterers and bakers ask for a deposit (for example 50% to 70%) before buying materials, with the balance on collection.

Rent and pay are often the biggest numbers in a woman's budget. They also involve people with more formal power than you: the landlord owns the property and the employer controls the job. Good preparation, respect and objective evidence help balance that power.
Two people agreeing on a property deal
Rent and lease terms are negotiable, and they should always end in writing.
Landlords and shop leases

In many Nigerian cities landlords ask for one or more years of rent in advance, plus agency, legal and caution fees. Each of these items can be discussed. Before you talk, gather evidence: ask three other tenants in the area what they pay, check listings for similar flats or shops, and note the condition of the property, such as leaks, broken toilets or no meter.
**Payment structure:** ask to pay one year instead of two, or a year split into two instalments with agreed dates.
**Repairs:** agree who fixes what before you pay. 'If I pay the full year, can the leaking roof and the door be fixed before I move in?'
**Increases:** ask how much notice will be given before a rent increase and whether the rent can be fixed for the first two years.
**Fees:** ask for receipts for every fee, and what each fee covers. Ask whether the caution deposit is refundable and on what conditions.
**For a shop:** ask about the length of the lease, the right to renew, and permission to put up signage.
Avoid rent scams

Never pay rent or fees before you have inspected the property in person and confirmed that the person collecting money is the owner or an authorised agent. Ask for the landlord's name and phone number and speak to them directly. Pay into an account in the landlord's or the agency's name and keep every receipt.
Tenancy rules differ from state to state in Nigeria. If a landlord's demand seems unusual, ask a lawyer, a tenants' association or a trusted community leader before you pay.
Employers: pay, role and flexibility

Whether you are being offered a new job or asking for a raise, treat it like any negotiation. Prepare your interests (pay, transport, working hours, training, title), research typical pay for the role in your city by asking people in similar roles, and list evidence of your value: results, extra duties, customer praise, sales figures.

Worked example: asking for a pay review

For example, Blessing works as a sales assistant in a pharmacy in Benin City, earning ₦90,000 a month. In the past year she has taken over stock records and set up the shop's WhatsApp ordering, which now brings in orders most days (approximate figures).
She asks three friends in similar retail roles and learns that assistants who also manage stock earn roughly ₦110,000 to ₦130,000 locally.
Her BATNA: an interview next month at another pharmacy. Target: ₦120,000. Walk-away: ₦105,000 plus a clear review date.
She books a quiet time with the owner and opens: 'I enjoy working here and I want to grow with the business. Can we discuss my role and pay?'
She shows evidence: stock losses reduced since she took over records, and a list of WhatsApp orders from the past month.
She asks for ₦125,000. The owner says ₦100,000 is the most he can do now. Blessing asks, 'What would make ₦120,000 possible?' He suggests a review in three months if WhatsApp sales keep growing.
They agree ₦110,000 now, a review to ₦120,000 in three months tied to WhatsApp sales, and Blessing asks for it in a short letter or message.
Blessing gained ₦20,000 a month immediately, a written path to ₦120,000, and kept a good relationship with her employer.
Talk about the future, not complaints

Frame requests around what you will contribute next, not what is unfair. 'Here is what I have taken on and what I can do next' is easier for an employer to say yes to than 'everyone is paid more than me'.

Timing matters in both cases. Raise rent questions well before the renewal date, not the week the rent is due, so you have time to look at other places and keep your BATNA real. Raise pay at a review, after a clear success, or when you take on new duties, rather than in a rushed moment at closing time.

When an employer cannot move on pay, explore other tradeables: transport allowance, a different job title, paid training, flexible hours for school runs, or a guaranteed review date. Always confirm what you agreed in writing, even with a short email or WhatsApp message.

Adapt to market haggling, family and community expectations

Negotiate honestly while still protecting your interests

Negotiation always happens inside a culture. In much of Nigeria, relationships, respect for age and status, and the warmth of greetings matter as much as numbers. A trader who knows you as a regular customer, or 'customer', will often treat you better than a stranger. Using this wisely is part of good negotiation.
Two people in friendly conversation
Greetings and relationships open the door before any number is mentioned.
Practical cultural habits
**Greet properly first.** Ask after the person's family or business before talking price. Rushing straight to numbers can seem rude.
**Show respect for age and position.** Use titles such as Ma, Sir, Alhaja, Mama or Oga where appropriate. Respect does not mean you must accept their terms.
**Build 'customer' relationships.** Buy from the same few traders, pay promptly and refer friends. Over time you earn better prices and first choice of new stock.
**Expect haggling in open markets.** Opening prices often include room to bargain. Bargain politely, smile, and be ready to walk to the next stall.
**Use language and humour.** Speaking the trader's language, even a few words, or friendly humour can soften a firm position.
**Fixed-price settings are different.** Supermarkets, pharmacies and many online stores do not haggle; negotiate there through bulk orders or loyalty, not bargaining.
Worked example: buying foodstuff at an open market
For example, Uche buys foodstuff weekly for her small canteen at a market in Onitsha. She needs a bag of beans and two baskets of tomatoes (approximate prices).
She greets the trader by name: 'Mama Chidi, good morning, how is the family?' and chats briefly.
Trader asks ₦95,000 for the beans. Uche has checked two other stalls asking ₦88,000 and ₦90,000.
Uche: 'Mama, you know I buy from you every week. Other people are giving me ₦88,000. Help me, make it ₦85,000.'
Trader: 'Ah, my customer, ₦90,000.' Uche: 'Let me take the tomatoes from you too. Beans ₦88,000 and the tomatoes at ₦18,000 each.'
They agree: beans ₦88,000 and tomatoes ₦19,000 each, total ₦126,000, with the trader adding a few extra tomatoes as 'jara'.
Uche saved ₦7,000 on the beans, combined purchases to strengthen her offer and kept a warm relationship that brings her small extras each week.
Ethics: firm, but honest

Ethical negotiation does not mean telling the other side everything. You may keep your walk-away point private. But you should not lie about facts. The difference matters, because trust, once lost, can cost you far more than one deal. In a community where people talk, your reputation for fair dealing is one of your strongest business assets.

Acceptable
Dishonest

You may hold information back, but you must not state things you know are false.
Spotting dishonest tactics used on you

Watch for sudden extra charges after agreement, 'my oga will not accept' after you have conceded (asking you to concede again), deadlines that do not make sense, or pressure to pay before you have checked the goods. Respond calmly: restate what was agreed, ask for the reason in writing, and be ready to walk away.
Family and community negotiations

Some of the hardest negotiations happen with relatives and friends: a sister who wants goods on credit, an uncle who asks for a job for his son, a family contribution for a ceremony. The same principles apply, with extra care for the relationship. Separate the person from the problem: 'I love you and I want to help; let us find a way that does not stop my shop from running.' Offer options rather than a flat yes or no, such as a smaller amount, a payment plan or help of a different kind. Where an elder normally guides family decisions, it can help to involve them early so that everyone sees the agreement as fair.
Negotiating in groups and cooperatives

Women's cooperatives, market associations and esusu groups can negotiate together for better prices, because a supplier will often give better terms for one large order than for many small ones. When negotiating for a group, agree beforehand who speaks, what the group's walk-away point is and who can approve a final deal. Report back honestly with the written terms, so that trust inside the group stays strong.
Online, the same culture applies in a new form. On WhatsApp and Instagram, a polite greeting, a quick reply and a clear price list build trust before any bargaining begins.

Fairness also means keeping your side. If you agree a delivery date, deliver; if you cannot, tell the other side early and propose a fix. Treat similar customers similarly. These habits make people willing to negotiate with you again and to send you new customers.

Most disputes come from a few missing details. Write the exact quantity and specification, not 'some' or 'the usual'. State whether prices include delivery, packaging and any charges such as transfer fees. Give real dates, not 'next week'. Say what happens if one side is late: for example, a client who has not paid the balance by the event morning does not receive the goods, or a supplier who delivers late gives a small discount. Agree who checks quality and when, ideally at delivery with both people present. Finally, if goods are collected by a driver or a family member, note their name and phone number.

For larger written agreements, both sides should sign and date every page, and each keep a copy. A photo of the signed document saved on your phone and in cloud storage such as Google Drive protects you if the paper copy is lost.

Sometimes the talk gets stuck. Both sides repeat their positions, voices rise, and nobody moves. A stuck negotiation is not a failure. It is a signal to change approach, take a break, or test whether a deal is really possible.

Moves that break deadlock
**Go back to interests.** Ask, 'Let's step back. What matters most to you here?' Often the stuck point is a position that can be met another way.
**Add options.** Change payment timing, quantity, quality, delivery or contract length.

Worked example: walking away from a shop lease

For example, Ebere wants to rent a small shop in Owerri for her hair salon. The landlord asks ₦1,800,000 for two years upfront (₦900,000 a year). Another shop two streets away is available at ₦700,000 a year, payable yearly, with slightly less foot traffic (approximate prices).
Ebere's BATNA: the other shop at ₦700,000 for one year. Her walk-away for the first shop: ₦850,000 a year, paid yearly.
She offers ₦800,000 for one year and asks the landlord to fix the shop's broken shutter. He refuses: 'Two years or nothing.'
She tries options: 'Could I pay ₦900,000 now and ₦900,000 in six months, with both payments receipted?' He refuses again.
Paying ₦1,800,000 at once would empty her savings and stop her buying equipment. The best offer is worse than her BATNA.
She closes politely: 'Thank you, Sir. It does not work for me now, but if anything changes please call me.' She inspects the other shop, confirms the owner and pays ₦700,000 with a receipt.
Ebere kept ₦1,100,000 for equipment and stock and left the door open. Walking away was a decision based on numbers, not a failure.
When emotions rise

If you feel angry, frightened or rushed, or the other person becomes aggressive, stop. Say you need a break, leave if you feel unsafe, and return with a trusted person or continue by message. Never make a large money decision while upset.
Re-opening after a break

Use the break to prepare, not just to rest. Look at your preparation sheet again, check whether any new facts change your BATNA, and think of one or two new options to offer. When you return, start with something positive and a short summary of where you agree: 'We agree on the quantity and delivery date; the gap is ₦20,000 on price and the timing of the balance.' Narrowing the problem to a small, clear gap makes it feel solvable for both sides.

If the other person was angry or rude earlier, acknowledge it briefly without blaming: 'Yesterday was tense for both of us. I want to find something that works.' Then return to interests. People often come back calmer once they have had time to think and to check their own alternatives.

Keep your BATNA up to date during long negotiations. If, while you wait, you receive a better quote from another supplier or another job offer, your position becomes stronger. If your alternative disappears, be more careful about walking away.

Walking away well means staying polite, thanking the other side, and leaving the door open. Many deals come back days later when the other side has compared their own alternatives and realised your offer was fair.

Why it matters

Not a talent: habits you can learn
A negotiation is any conversation where people who need something from each other try to reach an agreement.
Buying fabric, a customer asking for a discount, rent with a landlord, pay with an employer.
You negotiate at home too, about school fees, chores, or who travels for a family event.
It is not a talent some people are born with. It is a set of habits you can learn and practise.
The big idea
Positions and interests
Position
What someone asks for
I will only pay 40,000
One person must lose
Interest
Why they ask for it
A fixed budget, a worry, a goal
Options where both can win
The most useful idea in this course comes from the book Getting to Yes.
People usually argue over positions. A position is the specific thing someone says they want, like I will only pay 40000 naira. When you only argue positions, one person must lose.
Behind every position sits an interest. That is the need, worry or goal that answers the question why.
A supplier who demands full payment upfront may be worried about customers who never pay. When you understand interests, you can often find an option that satisfies both.
Getting to Yes
Separate the people from the problem
Focus on interests, not positions
Invent options for mutual gain
Insist on objective criteria
Here are the four principles in plain words. One. Be soft on the person and firm on the issue.
Two. Ask why, listen, and share your own interests too.
Three. Before deciding, list several possible deals. Different payment timing, a bigger quantity, an added service.
Four. Use fair standards both sides can check, like current market prices or the cost of materials.

Write these down before you start
BATNA: what you will do if this deal fails
Walk-away point: the worst deal you accept
Target: a good result you can justify

Many women lose money not because they cannot talk, but because they never decided their numbers in advance.
Your BATNA is your best alternative to a negotiated agreement. It is not a wish. It is a real option you could take tomorrow.
Your walk-away point comes from your BATNA. Never accept a deal worse than your best alternative.
Your target is the good, realistic result you are aiming for.
And the ZOPA, the zone of possible agreement, is the range between the seller's walk-away point and the buyer's. A deal can only happen inside it.

Every naira you save when buying, and every naira you protect when selling, goes straight to your profit. These are long-term relationships, so aim for deals the other side is happy to repeat.
Landlords and employers have more formal power than you. Good preparation, respect and objective evidence help balance that power.
Landed cost
Rukayat compares two fabric suppliers
For example, Rukayat makes school uniforms in Abeokuta and needs 200 yards of grey fabric.

Supplier B: 1,950, free delivery
B, 300 yards at 1,900

A low unit price can hide costs. Always compare suppliers on landed cost. That is the price per unit plus delivery, packaging and losses from damaged goods.
Supplier A charges 1900 a yard, all upfront, plus 8000 delivery. Landed cost, 388000 naira.
Supplier B charges 1950, with free delivery, and half now, half after delivery. Landed cost, 390000. Only 2000 more, and paying half later helps her cash flow.
So Rukayat asks B. If I order 300 yards for the next two terms, can you do a better price on the same terms? B offers 1900.

With customers
Protect your margin
Know your cost and profit on every item
Offer value, not price cuts
Use quantity breaks
Take a deposit for custom work
Customers often ask, what is the last price? That is normal and friendly. Plan for it.
If a dress costs you 9000 to make and you sell at 15000, a 3000 discount cuts your profit in half, from 6000 to 3000.
So offer value instead. Free delivery in your area, a small extra item, or faster finishing.
Use quantity breaks, for example 15000 each, or 42000 for three.
For custom work, many tailors, caterers and bakers ask a deposit of 50% to 70% before buying materials.
Rent safely
Before you pay any rent
Never pay before you inspect and confirm the real owner
Ask three tenants nearby what they pay
Ask about instalments and repairs
Get receipts for every fee
Inspect in person, speak to the landlord
With landlords, gather evidence first. Ask three other tenants in the area what they pay, and note leaks or broken things.
More than the amount can be discussed. Ask to pay in two instalments, and agree who fixes what before you pay.
Ask for receipts for every fee, and whether the caution deposit is refundable.
Inspect the property in person, and speak to the landlord directly. Pay into an account in the landlord's or agency's name.
Fake agents collect money for places they do not own. If a demand seems unusual, ask a lawyer, a tenants' association or a trusted community leader before you pay.

To remember. Compare suppliers on landed cost. Give value before you cut price. Never pay rent before you inspect and verify the owner.
Bring evidence to a pay talk. And keep your limit private, but never state false facts. Confirm every agreement in writing.

Closing
What every agreement needs
When gaps get small and the other side asks practical questions, like when can you deliver, move to close. Say, it sounds like we are close. Let me summarise what we have agreed.
Then check every point. Who the parties are, exactly what is supplied, the price, deposit and balance with dates, delivery, and what happens if something is late or faulty. Both sides confirm.
Worked example
Ronke confirms a cake order
For example, Ronke bakes celebration cakes in Lagos. A client orders a three-tier wedding cake.
Deposit, 60%, by Friday 14th
Balance, event morning
Includes delivery and setup. Approximate price.
After a phone negotiation, Ronke sends a WhatsApp message the same day. She lists the item: tiers, flavours and design, as in the photo the client sent.
A deposit of 60% by Friday to start work, and the balance on the morning of the event, before setup.
250000 naira in total, including delivery to the hall and setup. She also states when design changes are accepted, and that the deposit is not refundable after materials are bought.
She ends: please reply Confirmed if this is correct. The client confirms and pays, and Ronke checks the credit in her bank app before sending a receipt.
When it is stuck
Never make a large money decision while upset
Go back to interests
Add options: timing, quantity, delivery
Check an objective standard together
Bring in a trusted third person
Take a break and talk tomorrow
A stuck negotiation is not a failure. It is a signal to change approach. First, go back to interests. Ask, what matters most to you here?
Add options. Change payment timing, quantity, delivery, or contract length.
Agree to check a price list or a third quote together.
A respected elder or market association leader can help both sides save face.
Or take a break. Let us both think about it and talk tomorrow.
If you feel angry, frightened or rushed, or the other person becomes aggressive, stop. Leave if you feel unsafe, and return with a trusted person or continue by message.
Pressure tactics
What they say, how you answer
Price goes up tonight, pay now
My oga must approve
Small extras after agreement
I need until tomorrow to decide
My offer also needs final approval
Happy to add that, at a price
Learn to recognise pressure tactics. A false deadline. My oga must approve, after you have already conceded. Or small extras asked for after you agree.
Answer calmly. I understand, I need until tomorrow. Then my offer also depends on final approval. Happy to add that, and it will cost this much more.
Walking away
Ebere and the shop lease
For example, Ebere wants to rent a small shop in Owerri for her hair salon.
Landlord: two years upfront
Her walk-away, a year
Her BATNA: other shop, a year
Approximate prices.
The landlord wants 1800000 naira for two years upfront.
Another shop two streets away costs 700000 for one year. That is her BATNA. Her walk-away for the first shop is 850000 a year, paid yearly.
She offers 800000 for one year, then tries paying in two parts. He says two years or nothing. Paying it all at once would empty her savings.
So she closes politely. Thank you, Sir. It does not work for me now, but if anything changes, please call me.
She inspects the other shop, confirms the owner, and keeps 1100000 for equipment and stock. Walking away was a decision based on numbers, not a failure.
Track it
Score your result
For example, selling 3 necklaces, from the log in this module.
Score: 5,000 out of 6,000, about 83%.
Keep a log, one line per negotiation. Your score shows how far between your walk-away and your target you landed. 0% is your walk-away. 100% is your target.
Here the walk-away was 27000, the target 33000, and the result 32000. That is 5000 out of 6000, about 83%.
Also rate the relationship from 1 to 5. Over ten negotiations, if your score rises while relationships stay at 4 or 5, you are clearly improving.
